newsitem.title: USA: Hill conferees drop IDB proposal sought by Senate.
newsitem.headline: Hill conferees drop IDB proposal sought by Senate.

text.p: U.S. House and Senate tax negotiators agreed to drop a Senate proposal to increase the size of projects financed with small-issue industrial development bonds to $20 million, a proposed House/Senate agreement showed on Friday.

The move disappointed the muni market which backed the Senate plan and which, up until now, has seen few losses as a result of the congressional tax talks. The proposed agreement was published by the Bureau of National Affairs.
Muni lobbyists said they now will turn their attention to the next stage of talks on the tax bill - between Congress and the White House. They stressed that all provisions are very "fluid."
But chances that congressional negotiators will change their mind on the IDB provision at this stage are slim, they said.
Nevertheless market participants in general are pleased with the results of talks thus far.
Reuters reported Thursday that House/Senate negotiators agreed to drop a House plan to slash the two percent de minimis exemption for corporate municipal bond holdings.
Muni lobbyists now pray that the White House, which wants to repeal de minimis, will not press the issue further.
In other features, the House-Senate agreement includes some minor arbitrage rebate simplification provisions sought by issuers.
Also, House conferees agreed to adopt the Senate's proposal to repeal altogether the current $150 million cap on non-hospital borrowing by 501(c)(3) groups.
And House conferees accepted a Senate plan to increase from $5 million to $10 the arbitrage rebate exception for small issuers of bonds used to finance public school construction.
The Senate accepted a House proposal to allow refunding of certain tax-exempt Virgin Island bonds.
Senators also accepted a compromise proposed by House conferees regarding issuance of mortgage revenue bonds in disaster areas.
Under the compromise, mortgage revenue bond requirements would be loosened in Presidentially declared disaster areas for two years.
Negotiations between House and Senate conferees and the White House are continuing.
